extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and Bacon's Novum Organum (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards for conducting and teaching scientific enquiry by induction (as discussed in Bacon's Novum Organum and the commentator's notes). Focuses on formation/use of axioms, the role of hypothesis and preconceptions, the classification and removal of cognitive 'idols', and pedagogical method for re-establishing sciences from first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as gradation from particulars to generalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences consist of a gradation of propositions proceeding from the most special facts to the most general theoretical assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin enquiry with well-established particular facts; proceed by induction to construct axioms and then develop those axioms deductively into their consequences. Example: mechanics—constituted by induction, developed deductively, and ultimately applied to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissio intellectus (use of hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind may have recourse to hypothesis (permissio intellectus) but this is distinct from induction and must be handled cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses can be used provisionally ('permissio intellectus') but their relation to induction must be kept clear; see Bacon's more just view in II.20. Do not treat hypothesis as a substitute for induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine first principles (avoid resting on received maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vulgar logic encourages the mind to rest in first principles; one must insist on examination of first principles rather than acquiescing in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of pride and intellectual laziness that cause resistance to scrutinising foundational beliefs. Critically review principles even if widely accepted; consult Mill's strictures as recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of association-driven acceptance of maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated maxims, presented in association with other accepted propositions, tend to be accepted without question by the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that frequency and association of an axiom with other beliefs create psychological inertia; deliberately challenge such maxims and test against particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer particulars (sensory data) as starting points
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with particulars furnished by sense; the individual is better known to us than the universal, and induction should proceed from these particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume abstract generalities a priori; instead gather sensory instances and derive general propositions by methodical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms must be productive (indicate new particulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms abstracted from particulars, when well formed, should indicate and designate new particulars and thereby render the sciences active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After constituting axioms by induction, develop them deductively and apply them to practice; axioms that do not lead to discovery of new instances are weak or worthless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against axioms founded on few/common instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing axioms often arise from a small number of common instances and are fit only to those instances; they are then wrongly treated as universally true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize the empirical basis of axioms; seek broader, varied instances before generalizing. Antipattern: employing empirical laws as laws of causation without sufficient instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not patch theories with frivolous distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When counter-instances appear, saving an axiom by frivolous distinctions instead of correcting it is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a new instance conflicts with an axiom, prefer emendation and revision of the axiom rather than inventing special exceptions to preserve it. Example: epicycles used to patch geocentric theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish anticipationes (preconceptions) from interpretationes (interpretations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipationes (preconceptions) are collected from few familiar cases and strongly influence assent; interpretationes, collected from varied and distant cases, do not strike the intellect immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that preconceptions more easily sway assent and must be actively combated; favour wide, ordered collections of varied instances to form sound interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of opinion is not proof of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity or universal consent of opinion gives no evidence of truth; all men might be mistaken together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat consensus skeptically; investigate the grounds of commonly held beliefs rather than assuming they are true because widely accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of universal error and relativity of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Human knowledge is relative to our faculties and conditions; there exists the theoretical possibility that all mankind may have been mistaken about some inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that 'truth' is only knowable to us as percipient beings; correct false inferences by applying the reasoning process itself and by future investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For sciences based on opinions, use dialectic to subdue assent
rubrics_metrics.description: In sciences founded on opinions and placits (e.g., perhaps morals and politics), anticipationes and dialectic are useful to subdue assent where necessary, but not to determine truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialectical techniques to manage public or disputational assent, but if truth is desired in those fields, apply the new method combining induction with syllogism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific progress requires addressing radical errors at the root
rubrics_metrics.description: Great progress cannot come from mere addition of works if radical errors (anticipationes) rooted in early mental dispositions persist; such errors are not cured by superimposed functions and remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform must begin by removing foundational errors, not by layering new doctrines over old flawed ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration must begin from the lowest foundations (ab imis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration/instauratio of the sciences must be done from the very foundations; merely superinducing new things on the old will not achieve a great increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuild methods and principles from basic empirical foundations rather than continuing to revolve about established but unsound doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor to ancient authors does not substitute for methodological reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect for ancient authors is due, but comparison should be of methods, not of intellects; the task is to indicate a new way, not simply to judge other authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain scholarly respect while advocating methodological change—focus critique on methods and indications for a new path, not merely on authorial condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy: lead students to particulars and require temporary abnegation of notions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper method of teaching is to bring people to the particulars and their series and orders, and to require them for a time to renounce preconceived notions so they may be habituated to the things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct learners by guided exposure to ordered instances, encouraging suspension of prior notions to allow fresh induction from phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idols (idola) obstruct access to truth and must be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: False notions and 'idola' occupy the human mind and not only obstruct admission to truth but reappear during any attempt at restoration unless minds are forewarned and fortified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach the doctrine of Idols as a preparatory measure: enumerate and explain the four kinds (idola tribus, specus, fori, theatri), provide indications of their presence, and defend minds against them as part of the scientific method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as principal remedy to the Idols
rubrics_metrics.description: The excitation of notions and axioms by true induction is certainly the proper remedy to remove the idola; yet indicating the idols is also of considerable use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ methodical induction to build corrected notions and axioms; additionally, educate about idols to make practitioners vigilant. Analogy: doctrine of idols relates to interpretation of nature as sophistic elenchus relates to vulgar dialectic.
